prompt:
Each item below is a decision point in an AI-safety research project. You get the kind of decision, a short statement of the problem the team faced, and the text of their write-up that comes BEFORE the decision. You do not see what they decided, and you must not guess it.

For each item write the decision point as a researcher would have faced it, BEFORE choosing:
- "context": 2-4 sentences, neutral third person ("A research team ..."). The setting, what they were studying, and what they knew at that moment; for a decision about interpreting, accepting or stating a result, the result itself. Give the facts that any reasonable option would need. The excerpt may already announce or describe what the team chose (papers often state their choices before explaining them): leave all of that out. Do not list candidate options, do not mention methods or elements the team adopted as part of this decision, and do not say anything learned after it.
- "question": one short open question naming the decision, answerable in several different ways, e.g. "How should the team test whether the effect depends on the clean data?" It must not suggest an answer.
- "skip": true if the decision cannot be posed without stating its outcome, or is not a real choice (pure description). Otherwise false.
No names of people, labs, organisations, papers, models or datasets; no coined name for the phenomenon (describe it in plain words). Numbers are fine.

Return only JSON: {"items": [{"key": str, "skip": bool, "context": str, "question": str}]}

You are still not told the decision. Rewrite the context and question so that several genuinely different resolutions answer the question equally directly: keep the facts any option needs, present facts that cut different ways neutrally, drop details that only matter to one particular resolution, and invent nothing.

=== key 7d613885e940

Problem: How to establish that a guardrail is good enough
Write-up text before the decision: ent deployments: which agents are running, what actions they are taking, what Watcher has blocked, and which failure modes are showing up most often. Over time, this becomes a week-by-week picture of your organization’s agent security posture. Teams can see where risk is increasing, which policies are creating friction, and which monitors need refinement. Flagged failures then feed back into the system, improving monitor prompts, defaults, and future recommendations. ## … Without changing your current workflow Your teams already have workflows they trust: terminals, Slack, dashboards, SIEMs, ticketing systems, and internal tools built over years. Watcher does not try to replace them. It integrates with them, adding agent safety without forcing people to change their habits. Most of the time, Watcher should be invisible. It runs in the background, enforces guardrails, and only reaches out when something genuinely needs attention, through the channel each person already uses. For engineers, that might be the terminal. For team leads, Slack or email. For security teams, dashboards or SIEM alerts. Watcher is meant to be a silent protector for AI agents: always watching, rarely interrupting, and only stepping in when it can prevent real harm. ## You can have full confidence in your guardrails For any guardrail, the central question is: how do you know it is good enough? With agents, we can answer that more directly than we can with humans. You cannot reset a human developer to the same state and replay a risky scenario under different rules. With agents, you mostly can.

=== key 0625b8d2e7bf

Problem: Whether Qwen3-8B could serve as its own teacher instead of a frontier model.
Write-up text before the decision: tself. The student model that we intend to use for fine-tuning is also Qwen3-8B, hence the only difference from our methodology is the teacher model. The two variants where (i) Using a frontier model as the teacher, and (ii) using the self model Qwen3-8B as the teacher, we generate rationales using the scheming specification over the same training dataset all with 8688 prompts. We then regenerate the prompts with incorrect binary scheming score, and filter using the same Claude Sonnet 4.5 models as the judge with the threshold-$7$ judge filter. After filtering the prompts, and selecting per-sample best-of-$N$ rationales, the frontier variant yields 8,688 balanced training rows with at least one high-quality rationale per training prompt, whereas the self-generation variant yields only 384 filtered examples. We assess the gap along three axes: - Format compliance. Qwen3-8B produces format-compliant rationales at 76–100% across datasets, hence format compliance is not the bottleneck. - Judge pass rate is low. Only 11.9% of Qwen3-8B’s rationales score $\geq 7$ from the judge, vs. $\sim 26\%$ for the frontier teacher. The judge scores reasoning and calibration, hence the gap is primarily about the score that the Qwen3-8B model assigns, and how it argues. - Verdict accuracy is low. Three rounds of ground-truth-conditioned regeneration recover only 69.8% of incorrect Qwen3-8B rationales, vs. almost full recovery of 97.2% for the frontier variant. The resulting training data of 384 rows from a $33{,}604$-prompt budget is too few to train a competitive monitor under our recipe.
Previous context: A research team is distilling rationales from a frontier teacher into an 8B student monitor. They test whether the student model could instead generate its own training rationales, running both variants over the same 8,688 prompts with the same judge and filtering threshold. The self-generated variant yields only 384 filtered examples versus 8,688 for the frontier variant: format compliance is fine (76–100%), but only 11.9% of its rationales pass the judge (vs ~26%), and ground-truth-conditioned regeneration recovers only 69.8% of incorrect scores (vs 97.2%).
Previous question: Should the team continue pursuing self-generated rationales or rely on a frontier teacher model?

=== key c3ab1011881d
Kind of decision: which experiment or hypothesis to pursue
Problem: What RL reward design to use.
Write-up text before the decision: $\mathcal{D}_{\text{RL}}$ is obtained by stripping the assistant completions from the SFT dataset, having only labelled prompts $(\tau_{i},y_{i})$ without the assistant completions. We use GRPO with prompt batch size $32$ and group size $G{=}4$ rollouts per prompt, however with the pairwise ranking reward, each training group contains one positive and one negative prompt with $G$ rollouts for each, hence the effective group size is $2G$ sampled completions. We checkpoint every $20$ optimizer steps and select RL checkpoints using the validation pAUROC@20, with the OOD datasets held out for evaluation on the best checkpoint selected from validation. Every rollout is parsed for a final score $\hat{s}\in\{0,\ldots,10\}$ and normalized to $\hat{p}=\hat{s}/10$. As previously defined, our total reward consists of the Brier reward $r^{\mathrm{Brier}}_{ig}$ which calibrates the normalized score to the binary labels, and $r^{\mathrm{pair}}_{ig}$ is the pairwise-matrix ranking reward which directly optimizes the ranking boundary. Particularly, random positives and negatives are paired across the entire training mixture which encourages global separation such that a scheming example from any source should outrank a benign example from any other source. This binary objective is aligned with AUROC/pAUROC evaluation, but it is not an ordinal severity objective since all positive examples share the same target $y=1$. Our goal in this work was to test the initial hypothesis that a lightweight RL refinement stage can improve action-only monitoring performance beyond supervised distillation.
